title: The Last Undertow
premise: Ines Joubert has spent eleven years mailing postcards to a house that no longer exists, keeping alive a correspondence with a brother who died the night the Joubert family home burned under circumstances the town agreed to forget. When a radio station airs an unreleased song only that brother could have written, Ines realizes someone else survived that night—or someone is confessing. Following the song's trail through the town's complicit silence, Ines uncovers that their father, the respected magistrate who arranged the demolition, traded his son's memory for the family's safety, and that the song's singer is the fire's other witness. Ines must choose between preserving the fragile belonging the lie purchased and forcing a public accounting no court will ever hold, ending with Ines reading the brother's unsent letters aloud at the site of the burned house as the town finally listens.
about_author: Dominic Yarrow is the pen name of a former small-town court clerk who spent a decade transcribing other people's confessions before writing his own. He lives near a river that floods on schedule, and writes about the debts families carry across generations.

chapters.title: Poste Restante
chapters.summary: Ines's POV. We meet Ines through the ritual of writing postcards to a burned address, buying stamps from a postmistress who never asks questions. Establishes Ines as a tenant of their own life, employed transcribing wills. Emotional beat: the tenderness and pathology of one-way correspondence.

chapters.title: A Song in the Wrong Key
chapters.summary: Ines's POV. Driving home, the radio plays a song Ines knows was written in their kitchen and never recorded—their brother Etienne's unfinished melody, now finished. Ines crashes the car into a ditch and sits there until dark. Emotional beat: the dead reaching through the static; vertigo of a private grief made public.

chapters.title: The Magistrate's House
chapters.summary: Ines's POV. Ines visits their father, retired judge Auguste Joubert, who deflects with charm and wine, insisting the song is a coincidence. Ines notices his hands shake when the radio is on. Emotional beat: the performance of family; love as a system of managed silence.

chapters.title: What the Postmistress Kept
chapters.summary: Postmistress Sylvie's POV. Sylvie reveals she has kept eleven years of Ines's returned postcards in a drawer, unable to destroy them. She remembers the night of the fire—the trucks that came late, the magistrate standing in the road. Emotional beat: a bystander's long guilt; the town as co-author of the silence.

chapters.title: Demolition Date
chapters.summary: Ines's POV. A notice appears: the charred lot, still technically family property, will be cleared in six weeks for a municipal car park. Ines realizes the last physical evidence will vanish legally, finally. Emotional beat: a deadline imposed on grief; the state tidying what the family buried.

chapters.title: The Second Voice
chapters.summary: Ines's POV. Ines traces the song to a bar singer, Marisol Vane, who performs it as her own. Confronting her, Ines finds Marisol knows the lyrics' second verse—which only Etienne and one other person heard. Emotional beat: suspicion curdling into recognition; two strangers orbiting the same secret.

chapters.title: Witness, Age Fourteen
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. Flashback: Marisol, then a runaway, hid in the Joubert boathouse the night of the fire and saw who set it—and saw Auguste arrive and negotiate with that person while the house burned. She has carried the song as her only testimony. Emotional beat: a child's witness becoming an adult's weapon.

chapters.title: The Arrangement
chapters.summary: Ines's POV. Ines pieces it together: their father protected the arsonist—his protégé, now the town's mayor—in exchange for burying the truth that Etienne's death was not an accident but a message. Emotional beat: the family was arranged around a lie like bones around a wound.

chapters.title: Letters Never Sent
chapters.summary: Ines's POV, interleaved with Etienne's letters. Ines finds Etienne's hidden drafts in a storage unit—letters to Ines describing the blackmail, the fear, the plan to go public. He died the week before he meant to speak. Emotional beat: grief discovering it was also guilt; the brother was trying to save them all.

chapters.title: The Mayor's Handshake
chapters.summary: Mayor Delacroix's POV. Delacroix, polished and terrified, offers Ines a seat on the heritage board and a stipend to 'honor Etienne's memory'—a bribe dressed as recognition. Ines accepts the meeting and declines nothing, yet. Emotional beat: the seduction of power; corruption offering belonging.

chapters.title: Sylvie Draws the Line
chapters.summary: Sylvie's POV. Sylvie, pressured by the mayor's office to hand over 'undeliverable mail,' burns nothing but instead copies every postcard and mails the set to Ines with a note: 'Some addresses find you.' Emotional beat: a small civil servant's quiet rebellion; complicity turning to courage.

chapters.title: Family Council
chapters.summary: Ines's POV. Ines gathers their mother Camille and sister Béatrice and lays out the evidence. Camille knew—partially—and chose the family over the truth. Béatrice begs Ines to let the demolition happen. The meeting shatters. Emotional beat: the question the family arranged itself around, finally asked aloud.

chapters.title: What Camille Carried
chapters.summary: Camille's POV. Camille confesses she suspected Auguste's bargain for years and stayed to keep Ines from following Etienne into danger. Her silence was maternal, and it was a cage. Emotional beat: love as complicity; the cost of protection mistaken for peace.

chapters.title: The Car Park Surveyors
chapters.summary: Ines's POV. Surveyors arrive early; in the lot's soil they uncover the boathouse foundation—and a locked tin box Etienne buried. Inside: recordings, on cassette, of Etienne rehearsing the song and naming his blackmailer. Emotional beat: the ground itself testifying; hope arriving as evidence.

chapters.title: Auguste's Confession, Overheard
chapters.summary: Ines's POV. Ines plays a fragment of the tape to their father. Auguste doesn't deny it; he explains it—the town's peace, the family's name, the arithmetic of one life against many. Ines hears, for the first time, that he believes he was right. Emotional beat: horror without a villain; power's self-justifying grammar.

chapters.title: Marisol on the Record
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. Marisol agrees to go public, knowing the town that fed her for twenty years will turn on her. She and Ines record her full account the night before she's meant to leave town forever. Emotional beat: witness as gift; solidarity between two people the lie displaced.

chapters.title: Pressure
chapters.summary: Ines's POV. The machinery responds: Ines loses the wills contract, Béatrice is threatened with a zoning investigation, anonymous letters arrive. Auguste offers to confess quietly, to a judge, off the record—if Ines stops the demolition and the broadcast. Emotional beat: the system absorbing dissent; the price of justice outside the law made concrete.

chapters.title: The Night Before
chapters.summary: Ines's POV. Ines sits with the tin box, the postcards, and Etienne's letters, weighing the quiet confession against the public one. A visit from young Sylvie's granddaughter, who asks why everyone whispers about the burned house, decides it. Emotional beat: the next generation as the argument that ends the debate.

chapters.title: The Reading at the Lot
chapters.summary: Ines's POV. On demolition morning, Ines stands at the lot and reads Etienne's letters aloud to the gathered town, then plays the tape. Marisol steps from the crowd to sing the finished song. Auguste arrives and, before everyone, says: 'It was my arrangement.' Emotional beat: climax; private grief detonating into public truth.

chapters.title: Aftermath, Unarranged
chapters.summary: Multiple POVs, brief. Delacroix resigns; an inquiry opens; Béatrice stops speaking to Ines; Camille takes Ines's hand at the kitchen table. The town's belonging fractures and, in places, reforms on honest terms. Emotional beat: justice as rupture, not repair; the cost itemized without regret.

chapters.title: Return to Sender
chapters.summary: Ines's POV. The house lot becomes a small memorial garden, not a car park. Ines writes one final postcard to the burned address and, for the first time, delivers it themselves—to the ground. Emotional beat: mourning completing; the correspondence ending because it has been answered.

chapters.title: The Song Everyone Knows
chapters.summary: Ines's POV, one year later. The song plays on the radio credited to Etienne Joubert and Marisol Vane; children in town hum it without knowing its history. Ines, no longer a tenant, signs their name to a new will they're transcribing for a neighbor—and stays for dinner after. Emotional beat: belonging earned, not arranged; the undertow finally released.
